prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms confined at a magic wavelength are interrogated in parallel and reach a fractional uncertainty of about 1e-18.

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from circuit QED (B056) to the optical lattice clock (B052), and I want to be clear that the reason is the structure of the two cases, not the count of colleagues. The lattice clock is one invention with a physical mechanism that can be written in one sentence: a magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift of the clock transition, so that thousands of atoms sit in the Lamb-Dicke regime, free of Doppler and recoil shifts, and are interrogated at once. That is the step that turned optical clocks from a single-particle problem into a many-atom one, with statistical gain, and it has since brought a regime in which collisional and many-body effects have to be controlled and can be used. Independent laboratories on several species reproduce the roughly 1e-18 performance, and the clocks now test gravitational redshift at millimetre scales and constrain varying constants and ultralight dark matter. As a theorist working on quantum devices, I find the physics sharp. Its credit is two names, a proposer and a record-setting realiser, and it requires no exclusion that I cannot defend. In my own candidate I could not make that statement about the third place.
statement.case_against: The strongest case against is overlap and increment: the 2005 prize on the comb and the 2012 prize on control of single quantum systems and ion clocks sit next to it, and a sceptic can read the lattice clock as a further step in a precision-spectroscopy lineage. I think the citation must therefore name the magic-wavelength lattice scheme and its realisation, not clocks in general. A second reservation is timing, since the second has not been redefined, although I do not think the measured physics depends on that decision. A third is credit: PTB, SYRTE, NIST and the Tokyo and JILA co-workers built or improved the strontium and ytterbium platforms, and a two-name credit leaves them out. Priority details in this area are recalled from memory and not verified here. Finally, I give up what I still regard as the strongest candidate in my own area, so I accept that I may be underweighting the lattice clock's closeness to earlier prizes because I know the metrology literature less well.

responses.point: Kroll argued that circuit QED is partly quantum-computing engineering rather than a new physical discovery, that the 2025 prize comes from the same community, and that four names for three places is a credit problem he cannot resolve; the lattice clock has exactly two names and no recent prize.
responses.response: I moved on two of your three points. The Blais versus Girvin allocation is a real credit problem, and I have no evidence in the files that settles it, which is a poor basis for naming three people. On adjacency I still think that the 2025 discovery and the 2004 architecture are distinct, but I accept that, with an alternative that is clean on both counts, the committee has no need to carry that risk. On your engineering point I only partly agree: strong coupling to a single microwave mode is a quantum-optics result, not only a device. Your point has more force when the case rests on what later processors did with it. I take the lesson for the clock the other way: the citation should rest on the physics that the lattice scheme made accessible, and you rightly did not rest it on a redefinition of the second.

responses.point: Mehlig placed B044 first for conceptual originality and reproduced many-body physics, ranked the clocks seventh in the opening, and in round 1 called the clocks an acceptable fallback if the committee prefers attribution certainty to breadth. He also asked me to weigh my technical judgement on Blais versus Girvin seriously.
responses.response: I take that as a fair invitation, and my judgement is that the supplied evidence cannot settle it: Blais and Girvin were both essential to the 2004 proposal, and the experimental pair is the secure core. That is why I will not defend B056 as the sole prize. On B044, I think its physics is at least as original as the clock's, and I keep it as my second alternative. But in your own file the third place (Zoller or Esslinger) is open, and Zoller also overlaps with B009, so the attribution problem is not smaller than mine. On your question about what separates the clock from earlier prizes, my answer in physical terms is that the lattice is a many-atom, collision-controlled system whose stability scales with the atom number and whose many-body physics is now measured. A single trapped ion cannot do that, and the comb is the ruler, not the oscillator. If that is your remaining objection, please say whether it is overlap alone.

responses.point: Olsson prefers spherical-aberration correction (B011) as the most original and least replaceable contribution, calls B052 the strongest consensus candidate, and says a two-part prize would exceed the three-person limit unless B011's credit were split.
responses.response: I agree with you that breadth of support is not a substitute for merit, and I took the reverse step: I did not move because four colleagues prefer the clock. I moved because its attribution is clean and its physics is demonstrable. I also agree with your arithmetic on a two-part prize: B052 uses two of the three places, so a second part would need a single credited name, and I would not support splitting your trio or Katori and Ye's credit. On B011, I find the invention case real, but I think the STEM corrector lineage (Krivanek, Dellby) that you flag yourself makes the credit as contested as the circuit QED case I just gave up. Where the aberration-corrected microscope is a tool that opens new observations, I rank the lattice clock above it on physical reach, because it tests fundamental physics directly.

responses.point: Danielsson moved B052 to first place for the magic-wavelength mechanism and its reach into tests of relativity and constants, and gave a Schoelkopf, Wallraff, Girvin trio for B056 with the Blais tension noted.
responses.response: We share the same trio and the same worry on B056, and I now agree with your decision on the ordering. I would go further on the citation: it should say that the lattice scheme allows parallel interrogation of many atoms at the magic wavelength, which is what separates it from the 2005 and 2012 work, and it should not claim the redefinition of the second. Your concern about PTB, SYRTE and NIST is also mine. The chair's question about adding a third name is a fair one, but none of those groups is on the supplied credit list, so I do not think the evidence permits a named addition; I would rather accept the two-name limit than invent a third.

uncertainties: Whether the lattice clock will be read by the committee as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes or as an increment, which depends on citation wording that names the magic-wavelength scheme.
Whether a prize on the clock should wait for the redefinition of the second, which I think it need not, but a colleague with metrology expertise may weigh differently.
Whether Katori and Ye alone is defensible given PTB, SYRTE, NIST and the other platform builders; priority details are recalled from memory and not verified.
Whether Blais or Girvin belongs beside Schoelkopf and Wallraff on B056, and whether the 2025 prize bars it, which now matters to me only as an alternative.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged in kind. I direct WACQT and work on superconducting circuits and circuit and waveguide QED, and Chalmers colleagues Per Delsing and C. M. Wilson work in the same area, so I have a field-proximity interest in B056 and a documented connection to the 2025 prize community. If B056 stays under consideration I would defer to the chair on recusal and give my statements on it less weight. My profile records no tie to Katori or Ye or any other credited person on B052, so I do not recuse on it.
